canberra.title: Woman allegedly used blowtorch to light grass fires, police say
canberra.snippet: A woman has been charged after she allegedly lit a series of grass fires across two Canberra suburbs. Earlier today, an ACT Policing spok...
canberra.content:
The woman allegedly started fires in two suburbs. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

A woman has been charged after she allegedly lit a series of grass fires across two Canberra suburbs.

Earlier today, an ACT Policing spokesperson alleged a 27-year-old Waramanga woman had deliberately lit a number of grass fires in Fisher and Chifley yesterday (22 July).

At about 3:50 pm, police were called to Chifley following reports that the woman had allegedly lit the grass fires.

“Police allege that the woman used a gas-powered blowtorch to deliberately light at least four fires on Badimara Street in Fisher and Waldock Street in Chifley,” the spokesperson said.

A member of the public who said he saw the woman light the fires attempted to stop her.

Police allege she assaulted the man when he attempted to detain her, leaving him with minor injuries that were treated at hospital.

Two of the larger fires were extinguished by ACT Fire and Rescue.

Officers located the 27-year-old woman in Chifley and arrested her.

The woman has been charged with committing an act to cause public alarm and common assault.

canberra.title: Unemployment rates holds steady while more people find jobs, says ABS
canberra.snippet: Australia’s unemployment has remained steady at 4.4 per cent, with an extra 76,000 people gaining work in June and 67 per cent workforce ...
canberra.content:
Employment Minister Amanda Rishworth says Australia’s unemployment rate remains low by historical standards. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Australia’s unemployment has remained steady at 4.4 per cent, with an extra 76,000 people gaining work in June and 67 per cent workforce participation.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics released the employment data for last month, showing the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate was the same, but the increase in workforce participation was the highest since April.

ABS head of labour statistics Sean Crick said the 76,000-person rise in employment was driven by a 47,000-person rise in part-time employment.

“Part of the growth in employment this month came from those who were waiting to start a job in May,” he said.

“This represents a stronger June movement than has been observed in recent years.

“We also continued to see higher numbers of people remaining employed this June, following elevated levels in the recent few months.

“The number of unemployed rose by 13,000 people in June, which combined with the growth in employment, led to the participation rate rising by 0.3 percentage points to 67.0 per cent in June.”

The underemployment rate rose 0.2 percentage points to 6.5 per cent in June.

“People aged 55-64 years old had the largest annual growth in the participation rate, up 0.8 percentage points to 70.6 per cent,” Mr Crick said.

“The number of part-time hours worked grew 1.2 per cent this month, with full-time hours worked remaining flat.

“Annually, employment rose 1.7 per cent from June 2025, and hours worked grew 1.8 per cent.”

Trend employment grew by 0.2 per cent while hours worked remained flat in June.

Both the trend underemployment and underutilisation rates increased 0.1 percentage points, to 6.3 per cent and 10.7 per cent respectively.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers described the data as “strong job figures” and evidence of the Australian economy’s resilience in the face of global uncertainty.

“Helping more Australians into jobs is an important part of our economic plan, and we’ve seen more jobs created in the past month and more jobs growth in Australia under this government than any major advanced economy,” the Treasurer said.

“Even in the face of all this global uncertainty and volatility, unemployment remains relatively low and more jobs are being created, and that reflects the resilience of Australia’s economy and the progress we’re making together.

“More than 76,000 jobs were created in June, more than 1.3 million jobs have been created on our watch, participation is near a record high, and this Albanese Labor Government has overseen the lowest average unemployment of any Australian government in the last half a century.

“We recognise people are under pressure and we’ll continue to do what we can to ease that pressure with more cost-of-living relief, higher wages, more tax cuts and by helping people into jobs.”

Employment Minister Amanda Rishworth said the unemployment rate remains low by historical standards.

“Despite ongoing global uncertainty, employment continues to grow; the unemployment rate remains low, and participation is close to its record high,” she said.

“A record number of women are also in work, and female participation is close to a record high, which is good for families, communities and the economy.

“We have made a lot of progress, but we know some Australians are still doing it tough.

“That’s why we’ll keep working to create more jobs, lift wages and ensure people have the security they deserve at work.”

The reasonably strong employment figures could influence another rise in the official interest rate; however, the Reserve Bank of Australia might not consider a hike to the cash rate too harmful to the economy.

The next interest rate decision by the RBA will be announced on 11 August.

canberra.title: UPDATED: Corruption findings force Berry to resign from Cabinet, Barr apologises
canberra.snippet: 5:35 pm: Chief Minister Andrew Barr has apologised to the public for today’s corruption findings but has rejected any suggestion th...
canberra.content:
Yvette Berry will sit on the backbench. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

5:35 pm: Chief Minister Andrew Barr has apologised to the public for today’s corruption findings but has rejected any suggestion that there may be systemic problems within the government and the public service, or how the government conducts business.

He was speaking after Deputy Chief Minister Yvette Berry tendered her resignation on Thursday afternoon (23 July) following the tabling of the ACT Integrity Commission report into the Campbell Primary School modernisation project.

Mr Barr said the Commission’s findings related to the behaviour of two individuals, one in particular.

“The behaviour of a couple of individuals should not tarnish the reputation of thousands of people who work very hard every day within the Territory Public Service and in the Legislative Assembly,” he said.

Mr Barr said there was no link between the government and the CFMEU, given it was deregistered and no longer affiliated with the Labor.

He said a series of reforms since the Campbell School project in 2022 and 2024, including the establishment of Infrastructure Canberra and the centralisation of the procurement process for major infrastructure projects, made what happened much less likely to occur in the future.

He did not believe there were any further instances of similar behaviour but, if there were, any allegations should be brought forward and dealt with in the same way.

“It serves as both a warning to current and future ministerial officers and staff and across any political persuasion,” Mr Barr said.

“Unions, of course, have a legitimate voice in public policy and in debate and in occupational health and safety, but clearly a line was crossed here, and it was unacceptable.”

Mr Barr noted that although the Commission found no wrongdoing on Ms Berry’s part, she had accepted Ministerial responsibility for what had happened and willingly fallen on her sword, given the Code of Conduct was clear and explicit.

He brushed off a question about her position in the Assembly being untenable, despite all members of the crossbench and Opposition calling for her to go.

Chief Minister Andrew Barr says a line was crossed. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

He said interim ministerial arrangements had been made until the caucus met on Monday to elect both a new deputy leader and a new minister, followed by a cabinet shuffle.

Ms Berry would continue to serve on the backbench.

Mr Barr said the government accepted the findings in full and took them seriously.

“There is one very clear message, both for ministers and their staff: they have no role in the procurement process,” he said.

“Once a procurement is live, there is no ministerial influence or ministerial staff influence. That is appropriate.

“Equally though, for external organisations and individuals, they should not be seeking to contact ministers or ministerial staff about live procurements.

“I think both of those principles are quite clear and will be reinforced for staff and ministers.”

On consequences for Katy Haire and Joshua Ceramidas, Mr Barr said it was now a matter for police and the DPP to decide whether to bring criminal charges and for Mr Ceramidas’s employer, JACS, to decide whether he could continue in his role.

An ACT Public Service spokesperson said appropriate steps would be taken regarding Mr Ceramidas, in accordance with employment obligations. Any further action would be determined through official processes.

Mr Barr said his deputy’s departure from Cabinet was the end of an era.

“I’m certainly very disappointed, and very sad for the Deputy Chief Minister – the longest serving Deputy Chief Minister in the Territory’s history.”

He alluded to her being blindsided by her former Chief of Staff: “I think she’s been badly let down.”

Despite this being probably the biggest crisis his government has faced, Mr Barr said his position on his political future remained the same – he will serve out the term and decide on another term before the next election.

Ms Berry has represented Ginninderra since the 2012 election, first became a minister in 2015 and was elected Deputy Chief Minister in 2016.

She held the key housing and education portfolios.

3:42 pm: Deputy Chief Minister Yvette Berry has resigned from her ministerial positions, effective immediately.

She faced mounting pressure from the Canberra Liberals, ACT Greens and independents Thomas Emerson and Fiona Carrick after the Integrity Commission made serious corrupt conduct findings against Ms Berry’s former chief of staff Joshua Ceramidas and former Education Directorate head Katy Haire.

“The commission has made no findings against me,” Ms Berry said in a statement.

“Regardless, I have made the decision to resign from my position in Cabinet. I spoke to the Chief Minister a moment ago to let him know.

“I will sit on the backbench and continue to serve the people of Ginninderra.”

Ms Berry said ministers had significant responsibilities that she held herself to, along with high standards.

“Whilst in the report there have been no findings made against me, I will take full responsibility for the finding made about my staff,” she said.

“You know I have never backed down from responsibility, even when it gets hard. And this is no doubt hard.

“I have made this decision because I don’t want a parliamentary public circus to follow this report.

“My family don’t deserve that, and my colleagues don’t deserve that. And I have no intention of giving the Opposition and the Greens political party that satisfaction.”

Ms Berry stated her confidence in the government to learn from the Commission’s findings, and encouraged every MLA to read it.

She offered her thanks to the Chief Minister, her family, her supporters, volunteers and staff.

“I’m proud of what we’ve achieved together. We’ve made Canberra a fairer place,” Ms Berry said.

“I leave this role with my integrity and my moral compass intact and look forward to continuing to achieve more wins for a more equitable Canberra.”

The Chief Minister will speak with media shortly.

canberra.title: Man charged over fatal Anzac Day collision near Yass
canberra.snippet: A man has been charged over a horror Anzac Day collision that left one person dead and three injured. A NSW Police spokesperson said that...
canberra.content:
23 July 2026

Start the conversation

A 42-year-old man faces multiple charges. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

A man has been charged over a horror Anzac Day collision that left one person dead and three injured.

A NSW Police spokesperson said that just before 1:45 pm on Anzac Day (25 April), emergency services were called to the intersection of the Hume Highway and Yass Valley Way, at Manton (about 10 kilometres north of Yass), amid reports of a two-vehicle crash.

“Officers from The Hume Police District attended and found a sedan and a station wagon had collided,” the spokesperson said.

A 69-year-old woman – a passenger in the sedan – died at the scene.

The driver, a 42-year-old man, and two passengers – a 38-year-old woman and a 70-year-old man – were taken to Canberra Hospital.

The driver of the station wagon – a 32-year-old woman – sustained minor injuries.

Following police inquiries, the 42-year-old man has been charged.

He is facing charges of dangerous driving occasioning death, dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, negligent driving occasioning death, negligent driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, and not giving way to a vehicle (give way sign/line).

The man is expected to appear before Yass Local Court on 1 October.

Original Article published by Claire Sams on About Regional.

australia.title: Personal and banking details among customer data stolen in Origin Energy hack
australia.snippet: Hackers access Australian customers’ names, addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers and some bank account details, company says Follow o...
australia.content:
Origin Energy customers’ addresses, phone numbers and partial bank account data have been accessed in a hack, the company has confirmed.

The firm has 4.8m customer accounts in Australia, providing electricity, fossil gas, LPG and internet services to homes and businesses.

Origin has yet to confirm which, and how many, customers had been affected. In a statement to the ASX on Thursday, it said it would tell customers once it confirmed whether they had been affected.

A person claiming to be the hacker has reportedly contacted media outlets with unverified claims that 2 million customers’ details were accessed.

Origin said data may include customers’ names, addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers and Origin account information, as well as the last four digits of a credit card, or the last three digits of a bank account.

The company said incomplete credit card or bank account information could not be used to make purchases or access accounts.

Origin first revealed the hack in a statement yesterday, saying it believed credit card or bank details had not been accessed. The company has not detailed how the hack occurred.

Origin’s chief executive, Frank Calabria, said the company was securing its systems and ensuring there was no further unauthorised access, working with independent cyber experts and authorities.

“I’m sorry this has happened,” Calabria said.

“Customers trust Origin with their information, and I apologise for the impact this may cause.”

Experts have warned customers could be vulnerable if the data is leaked and used for identity theft, or by scammers tricking people into believing they are representatives of real businesses.

Rumpa Dasgupta, a lecturer in cybersecurity at La Trobe University, said personalised records could be misused for physical robberies.

“In the wrong hands, this information could be exploited not only for highly targeted phishing campaigns but also to support physical crimes such as burglary by identifying vulnerable properties,” Dasgupta said.

Origin said the Australian Cyber Security Centre, the Australian federal police and the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OIAC) were all investigating.

The National Office of Cyber Security is leading the government’s response.

The AFP declined to comment on whether it had identified or communicated with Origin’s hackers.

The Australian reported it was first contacted by a person claiming to have hacked Origin on Tuesday, after which the newspaper alerted Origin, which made a statement on Wednesday.

An Origin spokesperson said the company had moved immediately to update the ASX as soon as it was aware of a potential incident.

The OIAC reported it received 1,205 data breach notifications in 2025, of which 716 were related to malicious or criminal activity.

Among the hacks was a leak of 5 million Qantas customers’ information in October, which prompted warnings scammers could cold call leaked phone numbers.

The federal privacy commissioner last week found Qantas did not make any omissions or failings in breach of the Privacy Act, in relation to the hack. The Australian federal police are investigating.

australia.title: Pauline Hanson says domestic violence prevents police from dealing with ‘real crime’ in unearthed interview
australia.snippet: One Nation leader labels family violence leave ‘ridiculous’ and decries ‘woke’ support of women’s rights in November podcast Get our brea...
australia.content:
Pauline Hanson has described paid leave for those experiencing family and domestic violence as “ridiculous”, and suggested the issue is taking police away from “real crime”, calling for the family law system to be “wound back”.

In an unearthed interview, the One Nation leader said the advancements of women’s rights in the family law system over the decades had become “broken” because they favoured women and were now “suppressing the males all the time”.

The comments, made on the Broken Fathers podcast in November 2025, and first reported by the Nine newspapers, resurfaced as Hanson hit back at the criticism over her suggestion that domestic violence is a “two-way street”.

The senator has responded to the backlash by accusing the media and the Labor party of “twisting” her words.

In the podcast, which focuses on the perspectives of fathers during family court matters, Hanson said she saw the introduction of 10 days of domestic violence leave as “ridiculous”, labelling it a “holiday”.

“Ten days a year, they brought that in, so everyone’s, you know, claiming domestic violence and everything like that,” she said.

“It’s ridiculous.”

Ten days of paid family violence leave was introduced during the Albanese government’s first term. Under a program introduced in 2024, victim-survivors can access up to $5,000 in individualised financial support if they are leaving a violent relationship.

During the 70-minute podcast, Hanson repeatedly referred to the system as “broken” and in need of an overhaul, pointing to “feminist” and women’s groups pushing their agenda to favour mothers in family violence situations.

“I do think it is broken because we’ve got too many woke people in parliament now, and it’s pushing women’s rights,” Hanson said.

“But with … women’s rights, you’ve got to have women’s responsibilities.”

The 72-year-old senator, who has been in the political spotlight over the past three decades, also suggested the majority of police work was being dominated by family violence incidents while “real crime” was being overlooked.

“Do you know that domestic violence takes up about 75% of police officers’ time now?” the senator said.

“And that’s all they’re dealing with. And the police have had a gutful of it.

“They’re sick and tired of it because of the reports that they have to make, and that’s why we’re not dealing with real crime out there. The whole thing needs to be wound back.”

The Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) condemned Hanson’s comments on paid family and domestic violence leave as “shockingly out of touch”.

The ACTU president, Michele O’Neil, described Hanson’s remarks as “reckless and dangerous” and said people who use the leave “are not on a holiday, far from it”.

“Unions campaigned and won paid family and domestic violence leave because survivors told us they needed the time, so they didn’t have to choose between going to work to put food on the table or being able to make the break to safety,” O’Neil said.

Hanson’s previously unreported comments came to light after the senator was asked about her message to men who hurt their intimate partners.

“It is wrong but it’s also a two-way street. I’m not saying that it’s just men, women can lose their cool as well. Society is under so much pressure … Everyone is under so much pressure and it’s really hard,” Hanson told 4BC radio on Wednesday.

“Domestic violence is a scourge but look … I’ve been through it myself in my life. And I just feel if you’re not in a house where you feel safe … then you shouldn’t put up with it. If these women are getting abused by men out there, then don’t put up with it.”

After strong criticism from a number of anti-family violence groups, Hanson posted the comments in full, claiming “there is a concerted effort by some in the media to constantly take my comments out of context”.

“Some within rival media decided to use only a few quotes and made out that I downplayed domestic violence. That’s untrue, hence why it’s important that people hear the whole interview,” she said on social media.

Hanson’s chief of staff, James Ashby, explained to Sky News commentator, Peta Credlin, on Wednesday night his boss was trying to show “there is an element of domestic violence that comes not just from men”.

“Domestic violence is not acceptable, whether it be from a man or a woman, and she also said if you feel threatened in any way, shape, or form, get out of it,” Ashby said.

In a statement on Thursday, the sex discrimination commissioner, Anna Cody, condemned the comments as “harmful, wrong, and dangerous”.

“Domestic violence is never the responsibility of the person experiencing it,” she said.

“Violence is a choice – and blame rests entirely with the person who commits it.”

In 2019, the One Nation senator secured a controversial inquiry into the family court system, which women’s groups warned could become a platform for men’s rights activists who believed the court system was biased against fathers.

At the time, she claimed women were fabricating family violence complaints to keep their children. The claim is a prominent grievance among men’s rights groups but has been widely discredited in multiple studies.

In 2017, Hanson had told the Senate her sons had domestic violence claims made against them “that were not warranted” and said broadly “I feel for the men out there that are going through this, because it’s unjustified”.

    Welcome

What we learned, Thursday 23 July

That’s a wrap on today’s live coverage from us.

Before we go, let’s take a look at the day’s top headlines:

  • Australia is not ruling out stepping up joint patrols of the South China Sea following “destabilising” missile testing in the region.

  • Students in Victoria will be kept at home as a second teacher strike disrupts public schools, leaving thousands of families to make alternative arrangements.

  • Anthony Albanese has seemingly shut down prospects of a new tax on gas exports, saying he doesn’t interpret a Labor party platform document calling for Australians to get “a fair share” from natural resources as a call for such a new tax.

  • The prime minister also announced a new Fair Work court, which Albanese says will streamline workplace disputes.

  • Australia’s unemployment rate held at 4.4% in June after a big jump in the number of employed Australians in the month.

  • One Nation has been quick to capitalise on Barnaby Joyce’s viral moment yelling at his staffy-border collie Stella to sit down on live television by, you guessed it, selling dog leads.

  • Macquarie Group’s chief executive, Shemara Wikramanayake, announced she will retire in an ASX update on Thursday.

  • The sex discrimination commissioner, Anna Cody, condemned Pauline Hanson’s suggestion that domestic violence is a “two-way street“, warning assigning blame to victim-survivors is “harmful, wrong, and dangerous”.

  • The supreme court of Western Australia has dismissed in full a case brought by Woodside Energy against three activists.

  • The ACT education minister, Yvette Berry, has resigned from her cabinet role after a ACT Integrity Commission report found “serious corrupt conduct by two ACT public officials”.

  • The energy company Origin has confirmed customers’ addresses and partial bank account data has been accessed in a hack that was revealed yesterday.

Thanks for tuning in, see you again tomorrow morning!

Peak union body calls Hanson’s comments on family violence leave ‘shockingly out of touch’

The Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) has condemned Pauline Hanson’s comments on paid family and domestic violence leave as “shockingly out of touch”.

It comes after the One Nation leader described paid family and domestic violence leave as “holiday leave”, questioned whether it was “a scam” and said police were spending too much time on domestic violence.

ACTU’s president, Michele O’Neil, described Hanson’s remarks as “reckless and dangerous” and said people who use the leave “are not on a holiday, far from it”. O’Neil said:

Pauline Hanson needs to be reminded that on average, a woman is killed every nine days by a current or former partner in Australia. One Nation is wrong, and unions will not allow attacks on this hard-won leave to stand.

Unions campaigned and won paid family and domestic violence leave because survivors told us they needed the time, so they didn’t have to choose between going to work to put food on the table or being able to make the break to safety.

Former spy refused visa to give evidence at royal commission into Bondi shooters

Kat Wong

An ex-Asio agent who allegedly has information on the Bondi shooting gunmen has reportedly been denied an Australian visa despite the royal commission’s reported interest in his evidence.

The former undercover agent known as Marcus, had reportedly attempted to apply for a visitor visa in hopes of giving evidence at the royal commission on antisemitism and social cohesion.

He had previously told ABC that he had warned the spy agency about the two gunmen six years before the massacre.

A letter sent to his lawyers from the royal commission said they were “eager” to facilitate a way of receiving his submission or taking a statement from him, ABC reports.

But his request was reportedly rejected by the Department of Home Affairs over concerns he did not have a “genuine intention” of staying in Australia temporarily, saying he did not have enough ties to the country he is currently staying in to act as a significant incentive to return.

Information Rights Project, which is paying for Marcus’s safehouse in his current country of residence, has called on the federal government to reverse its decision, with its founder, Gabriel Shipton – who is also the half-brother of Julian Assange – telling Guardian Australia:

He’s facing credible death threats from ISIS and he’s trying to protect this family’s lives by being in this third country.

He really wants to come and give testimony as a whistleblower, he’s taken this big risk in revealing himself and becoming a source, and now the minister’s denied him a visa.

It’s bizarre and I hope they can reconsider.

Though he could give evidence to the royal commission from overseas, doing so would not offer him the same legal protections compared to giving onshore evidence, the Greens senator David Shoebridge said as he called on the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, to approve Marcus’s visa during a press conference on Thursday:

Minister Burke really has a choice now. He can choose to do the right thing and intervene in the public interest and ensure a visa is granted, and this evidence can be given in person to the royal commission with full protections for the witness, or refuse to act., let this refusal stand, and that will inevitably undermine the credibility of the royal commission and the credibility of the minister.

Burke’s office did not respond to a request for comment by the Guardian and the royal commission told Guardian Australia it would not comment on its engagement with particular individuals.

In a statement sent to Guardian Australia, Asio said:

Witness appearances are a matter for the royal commission, and Asio will support its decisions.

Ed Husic urges Labor to embrace internal party debate on Israel-Palestine

In the same Afternoon Briefing interview reported earlier, Ed Husic dismissed concerns that the party’s proposed position on Israel and Palestine would become a point of friction at the party’s conference because of “the way that debate is managed internally”.

Husic described his party as being “allergic to dissent and dispute”, but warned that this may not work “in our long-term interests as a party”. He said:

We have become so obsessed about not showing disunity, because we figure that that translates into some negative sense in the public’s mind. I’d actually argue the counter.

The public want to see politicians, particularly in our camp, stand up for something. We don’t sign up for the status quo. We sign up for change. That is not always going to be an easy process.

And the thing is, if you can’t argue your point on a conference floor or in a caucus room, how do you argue it outside?

Ed Husic calls for stronger ‘practical steps’ in relation to Israel

Labor MP Ed Husic has called for stronger “practical steps” from the federal government in relation to Israel and Palestine, on the sidelines of the first day of the party’s conference in South Australia.

Husic said he did not think “statements are going to cut it any more with the [Benjamin] Netanyahu government”.

Speaking to ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, he said:

They basically take them up and roll them up and ignore them, chuck them over their shoulder, ignore them. We do need to take a number of steps, and we need to take those practical steps.

When asked about his reaction to Israel’s embassy complaint ahead of Labor’s national conference on the party’s proposed position on Israel and Palestine, he said:

I do think that it is inappropriate and I do think that it is out of their playbook … And if this type of leverage that they seek to use, it’s quite frankly not right. I could never imagine an Australian government, through our embassy, our officials issuing such public commentary in that way.

Krishani Dhanji

Former Liberal cabinet minister attends Labor fringe event

Here’s a name you might not expect at the ALP National Labor conference … it’s the former Liberal defence minister, Christopher Pyne.

The former Liberal moderate – who calls South Australia home – is appearing as the now independent chair of the Council on the Ageing (COTA).

COTA is hosting a fringe event (a bunch of events that take place alongside the conference) calling for aged care reforms. Pyne is on a panel with a group of other advocates and experts.

Patrick Commins

Financial markets reckon RBA will hike by the end of the year

Financial markets now fully expect another Reserve Bank interest rate rise by the end of the year, with the chance of a hike as soon as next month doubling to 36% after solid jobs figures this morning.

The jump in oil prices after the collapse of the US-Iran ceasefire has been accompanied by rising fears of a fresh inflationary pulse as fuel costs climb higher.

Bets that the RBA will have to hike for a fourth time have now firmed after ABS data showed employment rose by 76,000 in June, even as the key jobless measure stayed at 4.4%.

Financial markets are now fully pricing in a lift in the RBA’s cash rate from 4.35% to 4.6% by December against an implied 80% chance before today’s release of the official labour stats.

Similarly, the probability of a hike on 11 August jumped to 36%.

But Taylor Nugent, a senior economist at NAB, said he believed unemployment would push higher through the rest of 2026 and that the central bank would stay on hold as the economy slowed.

Nugent, however, recognised that next month’s RBA board meeting would be “live”, estimating a 30% chance of a hike.

We think the RBA is most likely to stay on hold, but we certainly acknowledge these inflation risks are real and that in the near term they may feel compelled to lean against them more forcefully.

Krishani Dhanji

Labor conference closes day one sans drama

The first day of Labor conference is coming to an end with no major controversies or drama.

The second part of the afternoon began debate on the environment and energy security portfolio.

Anthony Albanese runs a tight ship in his caucus (ie there’s no room for dissent), and it’s clear a tight ship has been run at the conference too – known in the past for big fights and plenty of shouting. While we’ve seen a few impassioned speeches today, there haven’t been any spicy debates.

Tomorrow the conference will debate motions on gambling – the wording of those amendments is still being worked out but we know a few of the key issues will be around a national regulator for the sector and a ban on inducements. Those were both recommendations from the landmark, “You win some, you lose more” report.

Andrew Messenger

Queensland social housing wait times blow out to 31 months

The average wait time for a social housing dwelling in Queensland has blown out to 31 months, parliamentary estimates has heard.

The state minister for housing, Sam O’Connor, said the state’s social housing waiting list has dropped to 41,298 people from a record 58,927 people last year, though only 5,300 households were housed, with most applications cancelled or ruled ineligible.

But the average wait time for high and very high social housing applicants spiked from about 21 months last year to 31.7 months, the hearing heard.

During the estimates hearing, Labor tabled leaked documents showing the government had quietly cut $42m from its immediate housing response program, which pays to accommodate homeless people in hotels and motels.

The document revealed this would lead to less funding to a string of homelessness services including the Salvation Army and the Brisbane Youth Service, causing job losses. The document dubbed these decisions as of “high political sensitivity”.

The Department of Housing’s director general, Mark Cridland, told the committee that the number of people covered by the program had dropped from 2,150 households last March to 1,237 currently. He said 3,252 households had been found a home, drastically reducing the demand on the program.

Labor shadow minister Meaghan Scanlon told media outside the hearing that there had been no reduction in rough sleeping and “the only reason there would be less demand on homeless services is because he changed the rules, which has reduced the number of people who can now even ask for help”.

Read more here:

Origin confirms hackers accessed energy customers’ partial bank details

Luca Ittimani

The energy company Origin has confirmed customers’ addresses and partial bank account data has been accessed in a hack that was revealed yesterday.

In a statement to the ASX this afternoon, the energy company said impacted data may include: “name, address, date of birth, contact phone number and account information, as well as the last four digits of a credit card, or the last three digits of a bank account.”

Origin’s statement noted that incomplete credit card or bank account information cannot be used to make purchases or access accounts.

It said it would advise customers once it confirmed they had been impacted but was still confirming which and how many customers had been affected.

Origin has 4.8m customer accounts in Australia and provides electricity, natural gas, LPG, and internet services to homes and businesses.

Origin’s chief executive, Frank Calabria, said the company was securing its systems and ensuring there was no further unauthorised access by working with independent cyber experts and authorities. He said:

I’m sorry this has happened. Customers trust Origin with their information, and I apologise for the impact this may cause.

Origin said the Australian Cyber Security Centre, the Australian Federal Police and the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner were all engaged.

ACT education minister resigns after corruption findings for two staff in her portfolio

The ACT education minister, Yvette Berry, has resigned from her cabinet role after a ACT Integrity Commission report found “serious corrupt conduct by two ACT public officials”.

The commission investigated whether the process to procure a firm for the Campbell Primary School Modernisation Project was conducted with probity and whether public officials “failed to exercise their official functions honestly and or impartially”.

In a video statement posted to social media, Berry said she would take “full responsibility” for the findings relating to her staff, despite the report making no findings of corruption against her. She said:

When you are a minister, you have significant responsibilities. I have always held those responsibilities and myself to high standards.

I will take full responsibility for the findings made about my staff. You know I have never backed down from responsibility, even when it gets hard, and this is no doubt hard. I have made this decision because I don’t want a parliamentary public circus to follow this report. My family don’t deserve it and my colleagues don’t deserve it, and I have no intention of giving the Opposition and the Greens political party that satisfaction.

Berry will remain in parliament as a backbencher.

Luca Ittimani

Macquarie chair predicts fossil fuel funding will continue ‘for some time’

Macquarie’s chair has predicted fossil fuel funding will continue “for some time” as the company avoided a shareholder push for climate transparency.

At its AGM today, 17.9% of shareholders voted to force Macquarie to disclose how its fossil fuel financing aligns with its commitment to the goals of the Paris Agreement.

Glenn Stevens, Macquarie’s chair, told the AGM this morning Macquarie remains committed to the goals of the Paris Agreement through an “orderly transition” to green energy.

Ian Dunlop, a former chair of the Australian Coal Association and former executive and oil and gas company Shell, told the meeting Macquarie was backing “fossil fuel expansion” in practice. Stevens said in response:

The basis of Macquarie’s approach is our understanding that there will need to be some fossil fuel investment for quite possibly some time yet … The [emissions] targets that we set several years ago are the same targets now.

Kyle Robertson, the research director at Market Forces, the advocacy group that backed the resolution, said this afternoon:

Investors from across the globe have sounded the alarm on Macquarie’s fossil fuel finance, but many have let the group off the hook for enabling massive new gas projects which are hurtling us towards climate catastrophe.

WA supreme court dismisses Woodside case against activists

Petra Stock

The supreme court of Western Australia has dismissed in full a case brought by Woodside Energy against three activists.

The case relates to a protest on 1 June 2023, in which Kristen Morrissey caused approximately 2,500 Woodside employees to be evacuated by a hoax “gas leak” using “stench gas”.

The oil and gas company alleged that other people were involved in the protest and asked the court to order Emil Davey, Joana Partyka and Kristen Morrissey to reveal the identities of any other such people.

The three anti-Woodside campaigners had already been charged and convicted in relation to the protest.

In 2025, Morrisey was charged with doing an act with intent to annoy and doing an act to create false belief. Partyka and Davey, who were not present at the protest but were arrested in WA counter-terror police raids weeks later, were charged with doing an act to create false belief.

All activists pleaded guilty to the charges and were convicted in the district court of Western Australia.

Woodside’s legal action sought access to information about other people involved. But in a decision on Thursday, Justice Matthew Howard said the evidence and submissions presented by Woodside did not “rise above mere conjecture or speculation”.

Joana Partyka, a ceramic artist and campaigner represented by Climate Defenders Australia, said:

After three long years of Woodside’s legal threat hanging over our heads, we stand vindicated in the eyes of history – Woodside is completely humiliated.

The case was the first time since the “Gunns 20” in Tasmania in 2005 that a large resources company had sought to target an activist campaign using Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (known as a SLAPP suit).

Labor environment group passes amendment paring back fuel tax credits

Krishani Dhanji

The amendment is adopted unanimously and without any drama (none of the delegates vote against), which gets a huge round of applause from the spectator benches.

The room is divided by the 400 delegates on the floor and then spectator benches which includes media, lobbyists, and other observers.

There’s a contingent of around a dozen LEAN supporters in green T-shirts sitting in the room, who erupt in cheers as the amendment is supported.

But as we noted a little earlier, this doesn’t doesn’t mean that the fuel tax credits will necessarily be wound back by the government, even though there’s plenty of appetite for it within the caucus – and the rank and file.

A few MPs around the conference today say they’re hopeful the changes will be made at some point, but don’t think it’ll be done very soon as the globe continues to grapple with fuel insecurity due to the war in the Middle East.

New South Wales firefighters to help battle Californian wildfires

Two dozen New South Wales firefighters will be deployed to the United States to assist with ongoing wildfires hitting California, the state’s Royal Fire Service has confirmed.

The NSW contingent includes 26 incident management and specialist firefighters, part of a contingent of 74 people across Australia that were formally requested by the National Interagency Fire Centre in the US.

The group will help battle more than 72 large wildfires which have burnt millions of hectares across the United States.

The NSW contingent will head off on Friday morning.

Last month, three firefighters were killed and two others were hurt while responding to wildfires along the Colorado-Utah border. And a fortnight ago, a pilot who was helping to fight a wildfire in Colorado has died after the aviator’s aircraft crashed into a reservoir

‘Send a message to the haters’: Labor’s environment network pushes for action on generous fuel tax credits

Krishani Dhanji

We’ve arrived at one of the policy sticking points of the day – fuel tax credits.

The Labor Environment Action Network (LEAN) has put forward an amendment to the platform to “remove disincentives for orderly decarbonisation” – ie wind back the generous fuel tax credits that go to miners, farmers and other industries.

The group says 355 branches have supported the motion around the country.

Federal MPs including Sally Sitou, Jerome Laxale, and assistant minister Ged Kearney speak on the amendment.

Laxale says that Labor’s platform should “scream” that the party is serious about the climate.

This amendment and our platform should send a message to the haters that Labor can and Labor will double down on decarbonisation. Our new platform, our new platform, should scream that Labor are serious about climate action, and no one who reads it should be surprised when we use our time in government to deliver it. Our job is not done. There are new policies that we need to reach our climate goals and targets.

The amendment is quickly adopted unanimously (none of the delegates vote against) – which gets a huge round of applause from the spectator benches.

The room is divided by the 400 delegates on the floor and then spectator benches which includes media, lobbyists, and other observers.

There’s a contingent of around a dozen LEAN supporters in green T-shirts who erupt in cheers as the amendment is supported.

australia.title: Husic says Labor ‘allergic to dissent’ as he breaks ranks on key government positions at party conference
australia.snippet: Criticism comes as prime minister frames unity as point of difference to political opponents, saying ALP chooses ‘progress over protest’ ...
australia.content:
Outspoken Labor MP Ed Husic claims the party has become “allergic” to dissent and dispute, warning the unity on show at its tightly controlled national conference could backfire.

The former industry minister broke ranks with the government on the first day of Labor’s 50th party conference to support a gas export tax, endorse Indigenous truth-telling and press for more criticism of Israel’s conduct in Gaza.

As factional powerbrokers negotiated behind the scenes to avert contested debates on the conference floor, Husic hit out at the party’s culture under Anthony Albanese.

“This whole thing of being allergic to dissent [and] dispute, I don’t think that actually works in our long-term interests as a party,” he told ABC’s Afternoon Briefing.

In a speech to open the conference, Albanese framed the party’s unity as a point of difference to its political opponents.

“We choose progress over protest. We choose purpose over chaos. We choose unity over division,” he said.

Earlier, the government was given the green light from party members and MPs to wind back fuel subsidies for big miners, setting up a potential fight with resources giants.

The national conference also agreed to extract a “fairer return” from Australia’s natural resources, although Albanese shut down any prospect that would translate into a new gas export tax in the foreseeable future.

The Labor Environment Action Network (Lean) secured support at the opening day of the national conference to amend the policy platform to remove tax “disincentives” to an “orderly” energy transition.

The influential group of rank-and-file Labor members pushed the proposal as part of a campaign to cap the diesel fuel tax credit for mining companies, which they view as an expensive handbrake to decarbonisation.

More than 350 Labor branches, unions, climate campaigners and the mining billionaire Andrew Forrest have backed reforms to the scheme, which refunds miners, farmers and other industries the 52.6c a litre excise applied to petrol and diesel.

Treasury has forecast the scheme would cost the budget $47bn over the next four years, rising from $10.7bn in 2026-27 to $12.8bn in 2029-2030. More than $1bn a year goes to coalmine operators.

A trio of federal Labor MPs – Jerome Laxale, Sally Sitou and Ged Kearney – backed Lean’s amendment on the conference floor, demonstrating a level of support in Albanese’s caucus.

“Our job is not done. There are new policies that we need to reach our goals and targets,” Laxale told the conference.

“There are also tough decisions to be made to reform existing disincentives to decarbonisation.”

Senior Labor ministers were open to reforming the tax credits scheme before the US and Israel’s war on Iran and subsequent global oil shock pushed it off the agenda.

Albanese’s cabinet is not bound to immediately act on the platform and the government remains reluctant to pursue changes given the lingering uncertainty in the Middle East.

But the platform amendment will pressure it to act eventually.

Any move to wind back the tax credits would face fierce resistance from mining companies and their peak bodies, in particular the Minerals Council of Australia, which last month launched an industry campaign to protect access to the rebates.

Foreshadowing the industry campaign, Laxale told the conference that “reforming existing subsidies will be firmly resisted by the few whose profits are unfairly being boosted by taxpayers”.

It could also split Albanese’s cabinet, with the resources minister, Madeleine King, a public defender of the scheme.

Conference delegates rubber-stamped an amendment to the platform to secure a “fairer return” from natural resources, a set of words widely interpreted as setting an expectation for cabinet to eventually move to raise taxes on gas exports.

Albanese rejected that interpretation in an ABC radio interview ahead of the start of conference, ruling out any changes in the short term as the government focuses on shoring up fuel supplies amid the Middle East conflict.

The government also believes its plan to force gas producers to reserve 20% of exports for domestic users will effectively act as a tax.

Albanese’s stance failed to deter Labor’s most pro-tax MP, Husic, who challenged the government to show it has “steel in its spine” by adopting a policy that he said had widespread support in the community.

“Labor has a chance to be able to show, particularly to the broader public, that it’s got what it takes, that it’s got the steel in the spine to be able to make a call that’s really in the nation’s long-term interest,” Husic said at a press conference on the sidelines of the Adelaide conference.

“A lot of Australians reckon we’ve been ripped off. Labor can stand up, seize this moment, seize the money [and] also seize the agenda long-term.”

australia.title: Afternoon Update: Hanson calls domestic violence leave ‘ridiculous’; Husic urges gas tax; and orcas’ explosive hunting habits
australia.snippet: Want to get this in your inbox every weekday? Sign up for the Afternoon Update here , and start your day with our Morning Mail newsletter...
australia.content:
Good afternoon.

The One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, has described paid leave for those suffering family and domestic violence as “ridiculous” and suggested the issue is taking police away from “real crime”.

In an unearthed interview, Hanson said the advancements of women’s rights in the family law system over decades had become “broken” because courts favoured women and were now “suppressing the males all the time”.

The comments, made on a November 2025 podcast and first reported by the Nine newspapers, resurfaced after Hanson was criticised over her suggestions domestic violence was a “two-way street”.

Top news

  • Houthis claim strikes on two Saudi tankers as US attacks on Iran widen

  • Seinfeld’s Jason Alexander apologises to actor for ‘inappropriate’ sketch made when she was a teenager

  • ‘A statement of freedom’: T-shirt slogan goes viral and book sales rocket in Taiwan after Hong Kong raids

  • How do Lime’s ebikes make money? Share market debut sheds light on finances

  • AusAlert test will blast emergency warning siren over most phones in Australia on Monday. Here’s what to know

In video

Orcas have been observed ramming into giant fish so hard that the prey explode, possibly as a form of gory entertainment.

What they said …

“Labor has a chance to be able to show, particularly to the broader public, that it’s got what it takes, that it’s got the steel in the spine …” – Ed Husic

The Labor backbencher said he would join other delegates at Labor’s national conference in pushing the government to raise tax on gas exports – just hours after Anthony Albanese ruled out adopting the policy in the near future.

world.title: Two Russian men jailed in Angola for terrorism and spying
world.snippet: The men were convicted over alleged plan to stage coup and organise deadly demonstrations over fuel prices last year Two Russian men have...
world.content:
Two Russian men have been found guilty by an Angolan court of terrorism and spying, after being accused of planning a coup and helping to organise deadly demonstrations in the southern African country last year.

Lev Lakshtanov and Igor Ratchin were sentenced to eight and 11 years in jail respectively. They had denied the charges, claiming they were in Angola for cultural and business activities.

From 28-30 July 2025, a minibus taxi strike over fuel price hikes descended into riots and looting, in which 22 people were killed and more than 1,600 arrested according to official figures.

Angola’s security forces were accused of firing live ammunition at protesters; the government said its “progressive” use of force was justified. Human Rights Watch had previously said Angola used “excessive force” when it used rubber bullets and teargas to break up a peaceful protest against rising fuel prices on 12 July 2025.

Angolan prosecutors said Lakshtanov and Ratchin wanted to influence next year’s presidential elections, including by funding Angola’s largest opposition party, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola (UNITA), or by forcing a leadership change within the Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola (MPLA), which has ruled the country since independence from Portugal in 1975.

Prosecutors also claimed the men were linked to Africa Politology, a Russian disinformation and propaganda network that emerged from the Wagner mercenary group.

Africa Politology was taken over by Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) after the death of Wagner chief Yevgeny Prigozhin in 2023, according to an investigation by media outlets including Forbidden Stories. Wagner was rebranded as Africa Corps and absorbed by Russia’s military.

Angola, whose economy is highly dependent on oil exports, has historically been close with Russia. During the cold war years of Angola’s 1975-2002 civil war, the Soviet Union and Cuba supported the MPLA, while the US and apartheid South Africa backed its opponents, including UNITA. However, Angola’s president, João Lourenço, has improved relations with the US and Europe since taking power in 2017.

In the last decade, Russia has increased its presence in Africa. The Wagner group and then Africa Corps have provided security for the Central African Republic’s president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, since 2017.

In 2021, Wagner forces arrived in Mali to support the military junta. Africa Corps also backs the military regimes in neighbouring Niger and Burkina Faso. Since 2023, Russian troops have also been deployed in Equatorial Guinea, Libya and Sudan, according to a US Congress report.

Madagascar’s president, Michael Randrianirina, has also boosted ties with Russia since taking power in a coup in October 2025. There are Russians in his presidential guard and a weekly programme about Madagascar-Russia relations was launched earlier this month on national television.

Two Angolans were also tried alongside the Russians. Sports journalist Carlos Tomé received a two-year suspended prison sentence. Francisco de Oliveira, the secretary-general of UNITA’s youth wing, was acquitted.

Prosecutors have appealed against those sentences, according to the Portuguese news agency Lusa. Lakshtanov and Ratchin have also appealed against their sentences, but will remain in detention while the appeal is processed, Lusa reported.

Russia’s embassy in Angola did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Agence France-Press contributed to this report

world.title: Health worker monitored for Ebola in London hospital after working in DRC
world.snippet: UK resident was evacuated from Democratic Republic of the Congo where there is an outbreak of the disease A humanitarian worker is being ...
world.content:
A humanitarian worker is being monitored at a specialist hospital in London after potential exposure to the Ebola virus.

The UK resident was medically evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) where the worker had been treating patients with the disease, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said.

UKHSA said the person was evacuated as a “highly precautionary measure”, adding: “The individual is not currently displaying any symptoms and remains well, but as a precautionary measure they have been evacuated on a flight chartered solely for the evacuation.

“They are now being assessed and monitored in isolation by infectious disease specialists at a London hospital.”

The agency said the incubation period of Ebola ranges from two to 21 days and the individual will be closely monitored and is required to isolate throughout this period.

There are no confirmed cases of Ebola in the UK and the risk to the general public remains low.

Richard Pebody, the director of epidemic and emerging infections at the UKHSA, said: “This individual has been transferred out of an abundance of caution and we’re pleased they remain well.”

Last month, a patient suspected of having the Ebola virus at a Glasgow hospital tested negative.

Precautionary measures were taken after the patient was admitted to the Queen Elizabeth University hospital.

An outbreak of the disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda in May was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the World Health Organization (WHO).

The virus is transmitted to people from wild animals and then spreads in the human population through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs or other bodily fluids of infected people and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding or clothing.

According to WHO, symptoms can include fever, fatigue, malaise, muscle, pain, headache and sore throat. These are followed by vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, rash, and symptoms of impaired kidney and liver functions.

world.title: Healthy diet too expensive for one in three people globally, UN report finds
world.snippet: Global hunger declined for the third year in a row in 2025 but experts call for action to bring down costs of fruit, vegetables and dairy...
world.content:
One in three people cannot afford to eat a healthy diet, a new report has found, prompting calls for urgent action on food affordability.

There are 2.69 billion people unable to afford a diverse diet that meets their energy and nutrient needs, and it will take “immense” amounts of work to achieve the global target of zero hunger by 2030, the annual report from five UN agencies warned.

Global hunger declined for a third consecutive year in 2025, with 7.8% of people affected, down from 8.1% in 2024. There were also signs that a prolonged upward trend in Africa was coming to a halt.

However, the proportion of people who cannot afford a healthy diet remains “extremely high”, said Maximo Torero, chief economist of the Food and Agriculture Organization, one of the report’s authors.

The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026 report calculated the cost of a healthy diet is 4.28 purchasing power parity (PPP) dollars a day. This means that in any given country, a healthy diet costs the amount of local currency with the same buying power that $4.28 has in the US.

“The extreme poverty line is $3PPP per person,” Torero said. “So it’s significantly higher.”

He said government policies had typically focused on subsidising cereals and starchy staples, rather than meat, dairy, fruit and vegetables.

“That means calories, but not a diversity of diet,” he said, highlighting the impact of this on rates of obesity and diseases such as cancer and diabetes.

Figures from the World Health Organization, another of the UN agencies behind the report, show adult obesity rose from 12.1% in 2012 to 16.2% in 2024.

“It’s extremely urgent,” Torero said. “Obesity [among adults] is growing at a very steep level, so we need to now work intensively on trying to minimise those risks and those hidden costs that that substantial increase in obesity will bring.”

He called for investment in infrastructure, research and development. Modelling in the report suggests more efficient supply chains could bring down the costs of meat and dairy as well as fruit and vegetables. New policies to encourage greater consumption of fruit and vegetables could also pay dividends, he suggested, reducing the economic impact of health issues linked to poor diets.

In Africa, 66.6% of the population was unable to afford a healthy diet in 2025, more than double the levels observed in Asia or Latin America and the Caribbean.

Africa is now home to the highest number of hungry people for the first time, with about 309 million, surpassing Asia’s 292 million, the report showed.

The rise is largely driven by higher population growth on the continent, Torero said, with the proportion of the population going hungry actually starting to decrease “for the first time in years”.

“I think this is extremely important, because the numbers are for 2025, where already we have seen a significant reduction in overseas development assistance in the region,” Torero said.

Shipping restrictions in the strait of Hormuz linked to the conflict in the Middle East are likely to hit next year’s figures, he said.

The report is authored by the FAO, WHO, Unicef, the UN World Food Programme and the International Fund for Agricultural Development.

world.title: São Tomé and Príncipe heads to polls in tense presidential election
world.snippet: Incumbent Carlos Vila Nova hopes to defeat his former party and secure second term as independent Voters in São Tomé and Príncipe go to t...
world.content:
Voters in São Tomé and Príncipe go to the polls for a presidential election on Sunday as one of Africa’s least populous countries seeks to burnish its democratic credentials.

According to the National Election Commission, about 142,000 people are registered to vote in the tiny African state’s elections, approximately 15% of whom live in the diaspora.

Since gaining independence from Portugal in 1975, the island country off Africa’s west coast has built a solid reputation for peaceful, competitive elections. But this year’s vote comes amid a tense political atmosphere and a lingering constitutional crisis.

The president, Carlos Vila Nova, is running for a second term as an independent, rather than as the candidate for the ruling Acção Democrática Independente (ADI), whom he represented when he was elected in 2021.

The tensions between Vila Nova and his former party began in January last year when he dismissed the prime minister, Patrice Trovoada. Trovoada’s replacement, the former justice minister Ilza Amado Vaz, resigned after just three days, before the current holder, Américo Ramos, took office.

On Sunday, Vila Nova will be running against four other candidates including the ADI parliamentary leader, Nito D’Abreu. Another former prime minister, Jorge Bom Jesus, attempted to withdraw his independent candidacy, but missed the deadline and remains on the ballot.

The main opposition party, the Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe, is now part of a broad coalition backing the incumbent president, despite being staunch ADI opponents. Meanwhile, an ADI faction led by Ramos is backing D’Abreu. If no candidate receives more than 50% of the vote, the election will go on to a second round.

The businessman Domingos Monteiro, known as “Nino”, who has been president of the São Toméan Football Federation since 2015, was disqualified after the constitutional court ruled he did not meet the eligibility requirements. Monteiro was born on the island, but his parents never became naturalised citizens after moving from Cape Verde where they were born.

“The constitutional court is violating the principle of equal rights … It is time for descendants born in São Tomé and Príncipe to say no to discrimination, to the culture of xenophobia and persecution,” said Monteiro.

For voters, priorities include tackling government corruption, high inflation, severe youth unemployment, chronic fuel shortages, and frequent blackouts. Rivals of Vila Nova are hoping this will keep him from a second term and propel them to the presidency.

Corruption in São Tomé and Príncipe “is the greatest catastrophe the country has experienced in this half-century [of independence”, D’Abreu said at the presidential debate on Tuesday.

The country is seen as a trusted western ally for security and maritime trade in the Gulf of Guinea, one of the world’s biggest maritime piracy hotspots. It also has offshore oil deposits that make a significant contribution to its economy. Observer missions from the European Union, G7+ and the Community of Portuguese Language Countries are on the ground to monitor the polls.

world.title: ‘We are preserving a tradition’: how Ghana’s sensationalist film posters became collectible art
world.snippet: Hand-painted works are often wildly unfaithful to the movies they portray – reinterpretations that sometimes resulted in threats, insults...
world.content:
Sitting on his porch in Teshie near Accra, Heavy J dipped a brush into red oil paint and dabbed it carefully on to his canvas – a flour sack – adding blood to a knife being wielded by a man. Higher on the canvas, he had started on an outline of a skull.

Heavy J was creating a poster, but not as you might have expected for a horror film. Instead, it was for the animated fairytale The Little Mermaid. The man with the knife was not a killer but the film’s kind-hearted prince, Eric. The skull was also unrelated to the story. “We add more to make people interested,” said Heavy J, whose real name is Jeaurs Affutu.

Hand-painted film posters by local artists were a hallmark of Ghanaian film culture from the late 1970s to the early 2000s, used to advertise screenings for neighbourhood venues known as video clubs after organisers realised that the original posters were not attracting enough audiences.

Plot lines were regarded as little more than jump-off points for humorous and surreal flights of fancy. Artists working for different video clubs competed to make the best “forgery”, as they described their interpretations.

The practice began to wane around the turn of the century as more Ghanaians gained access to electricity and their own TV sets and video players. Many video clubs went out of business and painters pivoted to create other work. But by then the posters had attained global interest, popularised in books and foreign exhibitions, and old and rare paintings became prized collectibles.

There was a lull in interest in newly painted posters in the early part of the 21st century, but demand has risen, driven by online marketing and a receptive customer base of film lovers in the west.

Deadly Prey Gallery has been working with artists to preserve the culture of making hand-painted film posters, while helping meet the increased demand.

Named after an action film, the business was co-founded in 2012 by Brian Chankin, then a video rental store owner in Chicago, and Robert Kofi, a Ghanaian who, as a child, used to work as a “hype man” for video centres in his home town of Winneba and later started collecting and selling posters. They partnered after Kofi sold Chankin some works.

Deadly Prey Gallery works with 15 artists, including Heavy J, who has been painting posters for four decades, connecting them to online customers and shipping the artwork on completion.

Most orders come from the US. Old action, science fiction and horror films have the highest demand. Popular titles include The Exorcist and the Star Wars and Terminator franchises. And prices for commissioned pieces start at $600 (£450) and vary based on the canvas size and other customer preferences.

Kofi, who is based in Accra, is part manager and part editor. He identifies the artists most suited for each work, shares his vision of the posters with them and makes regular visits to their workspaces to review works in progress.

In a studio in Ashaiman, about 11 miles from Heavy J’s house, another artist called Stoger was working on two commissions: one for the horror film Poltergeist, and another for the experimental drama Gummo, which contains multiple acts of violence against cats and a scene in which a character eats spaghetti in a bath tub.

The poster showed three cats and a man in a bath with a plate of spaghetti in front of him. In his feedback that day, Kofi, speaking in Ga, a primary language of Ghana, told Stoger two of the cats were not aggressive enough and the food was too clean. “I want uglier cat scenes,” he later explained. “The spaghetti has to be dirtier.”

Stoger, born Benjamin Amartey, was a sculptor before developing an interest in films and becoming a poster painter in 1992. “I use my imagination to make scenes that will attract people so that they’ll love the poster,” he said.

The emphasis on exaggeration comes from an African tradition of “visualising the invisible”, said Joseph Oduro-Frimpong, the director of the Centre of African Popular Culture at Ashesi University and a poster collector himself.

“The posters’ audiences have not seen the film, so it’s impossible for them to know [whether they are accurate]. Therefore, the artists tap into what they call imaginative painting,” he said. “They will highlight these things and in doing so they incorporate things that are not in there. There is a kind of sensationalism to it.”

The reinterpretations at times resulted in threats, insults and even physical attacks from viewers who felt duped. Kofi laughed when he recalled an incident in the 1990s when people beat him up after they watched the action film Double Impact and realised it did not have a scene showing Jean-Claude Van Damme carrying out a beheading, as was illustrated on the poster.

At the Centre for National Culture in Accra, dozens of colourful posters from Deadly Prey Gallery are pinned on wooden walls. They include Jennifer Lopez launching an arrow at a snake in Anaconda, and a mouse coming out of Jamie Lee Curtis’ mouth in Halloween.

“We are preserving a tradition,” Kofi said of the poster-painting craft. “We are preserving a history.”
